questions.q: State the ICMR 2020 RDA for calcium for an elderly woman (60+ years) and explain why it is higher than that for an adult woman (18-59 years).
questions.a: The ICMR 2020 RDA for calcium for an elderly woman (60+ years) is 1000 mg/day, while for an adult woman (18-59 years) it is 800 mg/day. The increase accounts for age-related bone loss, reduced intestinal calcium absorption, and higher risk of osteoporosis. A wrong answer (e.g., stating the same value or lower) reveals the student does not know the specific RDA revision for elderly or misunderstands the physiological basis for increased calcium needs.

questions.q: An elderly man with hypertension is advised to restrict sodium to 2000 mg/day. He consumes 2 g of table salt (NaCl) in cooking and 1 g of salt from processed foods daily. Calculate his total sodium intake in mg and state whether he exceeds the limit. (Atomic masses: Na=23, Cl=35.5)
questions.a: Total salt = 3 g = 3000 mg. Sodium fraction in NaCl = 23/(23+35.5) = 23/58.5 ≈ 0.393. Sodium intake = 3000 × 0.393 ≈ 1179 mg. This is within the 2000 mg limit. A wrong answer (e.g., using 40% without calculation, or forgetting to convert g to mg) reveals confusion between salt and sodium, or unit conversion errors.

questions.q: Plan a one-day menu for a 70-year-old sedentary woman (RDA: Energy 1660 kcal, Protein 46 g, Calcium 1000 mg, Iron 17 mg) using food exchange lists. The menu must include at least 3 servings of milk/milk products and 2 servings of green leafy vegetables. Show the exchanges and verify protein and calcium.
questions.a: Sample menu: Breakfast: 1 milk exchange (150 ml milk) + 2 cereal exchanges (30 g wheat flour roti) + 1 fruit exchange (100 g papaya). Mid-morning: 1 milk exchange (100 g curd). Lunch: 2 cereal exchanges (60 g cooked rice) + 1 pulse exchange (30 g raw dal) + 1 GLV exchange (100 g spinach) + 1 fat exchange (5 g oil). Evening: 1 milk exchange (150 ml milk) + 1 cereal exchange (20 g murmura). Dinner: 2 cereal exchanges (2 rotis) + 1 pulse exchange (30 g raw dal) + 1 other vegetable exchange (100 g bottle gourd) + 1 fat exchange (5 g oil). Total milk exchanges = 3 (450 ml milk + 100 g curd ≈ 550 ml equivalent). Protein: cereals (5×6=30g) + pulses (2×6=12g) + milk (3×4=12g) ≈ 54g (meets 46g). Calcium: milk (3×120=360mg from 150ml each? Actually 150ml milk gives ~180mg, 100g curd ~120mg, total milk exchanges ~500mg) + GLV (100g spinach ~100mg) + cereals/pulses ~200mg = ~800mg, slightly short of 1000mg. Need to add 1 more milk exchange or ragi. A wrong answer reveals inability to use exchange lists, miscalculation of nutrient totals, or ignoring the milk/GLV serving constraints.

questions.q: Compare the nutrient density requirements of an elderly person with a sedentary adult. Explain why nutrient density becomes more critical with age, using the concept of energy requirement reduction versus micronutrient requirement maintenance.
questions.a: Energy requirement decreases by ~200-300 kcal/day due to lower BMR and activity, but micronutrient needs (calcium, vitamin D, B12, fibre) stay same or increase. Therefore, each kcal must deliver more micronutrients — i.e., higher nutrient density. Choosing whole grains over refined, milk over tea, vegetables over sweets. A wrong answer that only says "elderly need more nutrients" without linking to energy reduction shows lack of understanding of nutrient density concept.

questions.q: Evaluate the following statement: "Since elderly people eat less, giving them concentrated sweets and fried snacks is a good way to ensure they get enough calories." Provide two physiological reasons why this is harmful.
questions.a: The statement is harmful. Reason 1: Elderly have impaired glucose tolerance and higher diabetes risk; concentrated sweets cause blood sugar spikes. Reason 2: Fried snacks provide empty calories and saturated/trans fats, worsening lipid profile and cardiovascular risk, while displacing nutrient-dense foods needed for protein, calcium, fibre. A wrong answer that agrees or gives only one reason shows failure to evaluate dietary quality vs quantity and ignorance of metabolic changes.

questions.q: Create a weekly meal planning checklist for a low-income elderly couple (both 70+, one with arthritis, one with early dementia) that addresses: (a) budget-friendly nutrient-dense foods, (b) texture modifications for chewing difficulty, (c) meal frequency and hydration reminders, (d) use of community resources (e.g., Annapurna scheme, mid-day meals for elderly). Present as a bullet-point checklist.
questions.a:
Checklist: 
- Staples: Buy whole wheat, rice, millets (ragi, jowar) in bulk from PDS; include ragi for calcium.
- Protein: Daily dal (rotate moong, masoor, chana), weekly egg (if non-veg), soya nuggets, roasted chana as snack.
- Milk: 300 ml/day each via curd, buttermilk, milk in tea/porridge; use double-toned milk to save cost.
- Vegetables: Seasonal GLV (spinach, amaranth) 3-4 times/week; pressure-cook and mash for soft texture.
- Fruits: Banana, guava, papaya (soft, cheap, high fibre/vit C); stew apple/pear if chewing hard.
- Fats: 15-20 g/day visible fat (mustard oil, ghee); limit fried foods.
- Texture: All vegetables pressure-cooked and mashed; rotis softened with dal/curd; khichdi, dalia, upma, idli preferred.
- Meals: 6 small meals (breakfast, mid-morning, lunch, evening, dinner, bedtime milk); water/buttermilk offered every 2 hours.
- Hydration: 1.5-2 L fluids/day; include soups, rasam, buttermilk.
- Community: Enroll in nearest Annapurna/old age meal programme; use Anganwadi for supplementary nutrition; coordinate with ASHA worker for health check-ups.
- Budget: Plan weekly menu, buy weekly, cook in batches, use leftovers creatively (e.g., leftover dal -> paratha stuffing).
A poor answer misses texture, hydration, community resources, or gives generic advice not tailored to arthritis/dementia.
